Store
stor
n. and v.t. (a stock laid up; to lay up in reserve; rendering Hebrew otsar, micken, Greek thesaurizo, apothesaurizo)
From Old French estor, from Latin instaurare, to restore or provide. Scripture's attitude to a store is not simple — Joseph's granaries save a world, and the rich fool's barns damn a man, and the difference is not in the quantity.

Biblical Definition

To lay up in store is to set aside a reserve, and Scripture treats the practice as good, dangerous, or commanded depending entirely on what the reserve is for. It is commanded for the poor: Paul's collection instruction is the New Testament's clearest word on systematic giving — “Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him, that there be no gatherings when I come” (1 Corinthians 16:2). Four things are in that sentence: giving is weekly, individual, proportionate to income, and planned rather than impulsive. It is commanded for eternity, and paradoxically the storing is done by giving away: the rich are charged to be rich in good works, ready to distribute, “Laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come, that they may lay hold on eternal life” (1 Timothy 6:19). Under the old covenant the storehouse is the temple treasury, and Malachi's challenge is unique in Scripture for inviting a test: “Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith” (Malachi 3:10). And Joseph's store cities preserved Egypt and the covenant family through seven years of famine — providence working through an administrator with warehouses. Against all this stands the barn-building of Luke 12, where a man stores for himself and is not rich toward God.

Webster 1828 Definition

A reserve laid up, good or damning depending on its end. Paul commands weekly, proportionate laying-by for the poor; Timothy's rich lay up a foundation by giving away; Malachi invites a test at the storehouse; and the rich fool builds barns for himself.

STORE, n. [Old Fr. estor.] A large number or quantity; a great plenty; abundance.

2. A stock provided; a large quantity collected for supply; hence, abundance.

3. A store-house; a magazine; a warehouse.

STORE, v.t. To furnish; to supply; to replenish.

4. To lay up in store; to reposit in a store or warehouse for preservation. Lay by him in store. 1 Cor. 16.

Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 16:2 — "Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him, that there be no gatherings when I come."

1 Timothy 6:19 — "Laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come, that they may lay hold on eternal life."

Malachi 3:10 — "Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it."

Luke 12:21 — "So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God."

Modern Corruption

Malachi 3:10 has been made the engine of a giving-to-get transaction, in which the tithe is an investment with a promised return — while 1 Corinthians 16:2, the plainer and more demanding text, is rarely preached at all.

expand to see more

Malachi 3:10 is the prosperity movement's foundational text, and its use there inverts the passage. The chapter is an indictment: a nation is robbing God by withholding tithes and offerings, and is under a curse for it. The invitation to prove God is the offer of restored covenant blessing to a repentant people, framed in the agricultural terms of Deuteronomy 28 — rain in season, the devourer rebuked, the vine not casting her fruit. It is not a formula by which any individual may treat God as a fund manager. The corruption is exposed by what it asks: a man who gives in order to receive has not given at all, and the arrangement makes God a debtor, which Romans 11:35 flatly denies. The dictionary affirms generous, sacrificial, and proportionate giving as the plain duty of every Christian, and denies that God has promised a financial return on it.

The more interesting fact is which text goes unpreached. 1 Corinthians 16:2 is more demanding than the tithe-as-investment scheme in every respect, and it is largely absent from pulpits that quote Malachi weekly. It requires that giving be regular — the first day of every week; universal — every one of you, not merely the prosperous; proportionate — as God hath prospered him, so that the amount rises with income; and planned — laid by in advance, so that the offering is a decision made at the desk rather than an impulse in the pew. A congregation that adopted that verse alone would give more, more consistently, and with less manipulation than any appeal to Malachi has ever produced. And 1 Timothy 6:19 supplies the motive that keeps it from becoming mere duty: the storing that lasts is done by distributing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew otsar (a treasury, storehouse) and miskenoth (store cities, as Pithom and Raamses); Greek thesaurizo (to lay up treasure) and apothesaurizo (to store away, the verb in 1 Timothy 6:19).

expand to see more

Hebrew otsar (H214) — a treasury, storehouse; the word in Malachi 3:10 and of the temple treasuries.

Hebrew miskenoth (H4543) — store cities, magazines; the cities Israel built for Pharaoh in Exodus 1:11.

Greek thesaurizo (G2343) — to lay up treasure, hoard; the verb in Matthew 6:19-20 and 1 Corinthians 16:2.

Greek apothesaurizo (G597) — to store away, treasure up for oneself; a hapax at 1 Timothy 6:19.

Greek euodoo (G2137) — to prosper, be led along a good road; the verb in 1 Corinthians 16:2 rendered as God hath prospered him.

Usage

"“Lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him” — weekly, individual, proportionate, and planned."

"“Laying up in store for themselves a good foundation” — the storing is accomplished by the distributing."

"“Prove me now herewith” — a covenant invitation to a repentant nation, not a formula for personal return."
